units.title: Argument: Precise Claims, Fair Counterclaims and Audience
skills: Introduce a precise claim and distinguish it from alternate or opposing claims
Develop claims and counterclaims fairly, noting the strengths and limitations of each
Anticipate the audience’s knowledge, concerns and possible biases
Use words, phrases and clauses to link major sections and create cohesion
vocab: precise claim
a specific, arguable statement of the writer’s position
counterclaim
an opposing position that a fair argument presents accurately and answers
limitation
a weakness or condition that reduces how far a claim or piece of evidence applies
audience
the readers a writer must inform or persuade, with their own knowledge and concerns
bias
a one-sided view that can lead to an unfair judgment
objective tone
a calm, fair voice that relies on evidence rather than emotion or insults

passage.title: Age Limits for Social Media
passage.intro: Lulu is writing an argument essay for the debate club. Read her draft and answer the questions.
paras: (1) Social media is a big topic. (2) Many platforms require users to be at least thirteen, but younger children often sign up anyway. (3) Research has linked heavy social media use among young teens to poorer sleep and lower self-esteem. (4) Stronger age checks would give children more time to develop before facing online pressure. (5) Critics point out that age checks could require users to share private information, such as identity documents. (6) This concern is reasonable, so any system must protect personal data carefully. (7) Even with this limitation, stronger age limits would better protect young users.

items.stem: Which revision of sentence 1 states a precise claim?
options: Social media has good parts and bad parts, and people have many different opinions about it.
Social media is a big topic that many people talk about and think about every single day.
Social media platforms should enforce their minimum age of thirteen with stronger age checks.
Social media is something that I use, and my friends and my cousins use it a lot too.
items.skill: States a clear claim or thesis

items.stem: How does sentence 6 treat the counterclaim in sentence 5?
options: It agrees that age checks should be removed completely.
It admits the concern is valid and explains how to address it.
It attacks the critics instead of discussing their reasons.
It ignores the concern and repeats the original claim.
items.skill: Acknowledges and answers an opposing claim

items.stem: Which transition would BEST begin sentence 4 to link it to the evidence in sentence 3?
options: For this reason,
Even so,
In contrast,
For instance,
items.skill: Chooses a transition that connects ideas

items.stem: Which evidence would BEST support sentence 2?
options: Many adults use social media to read the news and to follow their favorite sports teams.
Children enjoy playing outside, reading books and spending time with their families.
Social media platforms were originally created to help people share photos and messages with friends.
One survey found that nearly 40 percent of children aged eight to twelve had used social media.
items.skill: Chooses relevant evidence to support a point

items.stem: Lulu’s audience includes parents who use social media to stay in touch with family. Which sentence would BEST address their concerns?
options: Most parents do not understand how social media works, so their opinions do not really matter.
Stronger age limits would not affect adults, who could continue to use these platforms as they do now.
Parents should stop using social media completely, since it is harmful to everyone who uses it regularly.
Parents who use social media are setting a bad example and should feel guilty about it.
items.skill: Chooses language that fits the purpose and audience

items.stem: Which word in sentence 7 shows that Lulu recognizes a weakness in her argument?
options: young
protect
stronger
limitation
items.skill: Acknowledges and answers an opposing claim

passage.title: Electric Vehicles: Promise and Challenges
passage.intro: Ziyad is writing an informative report with headings. Read his draft and answer the questions.
paras: **Benefits**

(1) Electric vehicles, or EVs, run on batteries instead of gasoline. (2) Because they produce no exhaust, EVs can improve air quality in crowded cities. (3) They are also quieter and often cheaper to maintain.
**Challenges**

(4) EV batteries require minerals such as lithium, which must be mined. (5) Charging stations are still limited in many regions. (6) Furthermore, if electricity comes from burning coal, the environmental benefit is reduced.
**Looking Ahead**
(7) As battery technology improves and clean energy grows, EVs may become the most common cars on the road.

passage.title: Research Notes: How Arabic Numerals Reached Europe
passage.intro: Majed is writing a research paper. Read the sources and his draft, then answer the questions.
paras: **Source 1** (an encyclopedia of mathematics, 2018): “The numerals 0–9 were developed in India. Scholars in Baghdad, including al-Khwarizmi, described the system in the ninth century.”
**Source 2** (a museum website on the history of science): “In 1202, the Italian mathematician Fibonacci published Liber Abaci, a book that introduced these numerals to many European readers.”
**Source 3** (an anonymous social media post): “Arabic numerals were invented by the Romans and are the oldest numbers in the world.”
**Draft**

(1) The numbers we use every day have traveled a long way. (2) They were first developed in India. (3) In the ninth century, scholars in Baghdad wrote about the system. (4) Later, Fibonacci helped spread the numerals in Europe through his book. (5) Before this, many Europeans used Roman numerals, which made calculation difficult. (6) Today, the system is used almost everywhere in the world.

items.stem: Which source is the LEAST reliable?
options: Source 1, because it mentions the city of Baghdad
Source 2, because it comes from a museum website
Source 3, because it has no author and contradicts the other sources
Source 1, because it is an encyclopedia that was published in 2018 by experts
items.skill: Chooses a useful source or research question

items.skill: Chooses an effective introduction

Later, Fibonacci’s 1202 book Liber Abaci “introduced these numerals to many European readers” (Museum of Science).

items.skill: Paraphrases or cites a source correctly

units.title: Phrases and Clauses for Meaning and Variety
skills: Identify appositive, participial, prepositional and absolute phrases
Identify noun, relative and adverbial clauses and explain their function
Use phrases and clauses to combine ideas and vary sentences
Fix sentences in which clauses are joined incorrectly
vocab: absolute phrase
a noun plus a modifier that describes the whole sentence: Her hands trembling, she opened the letter.
appositive phrase
a noun phrase that renames another noun: my uncle, a skilled carpenter,
noun clause
a dependent clause that acts as a noun: What she said surprised us.
relative clause
a dependent clause beginning with who, which or that that describes a noun
adverbial clause
a dependent clause that tells when, why, how or under what condition
sentence variety
mixing sentence lengths and structures to keep writing clear and interesting
